argument: Camus's The Fall extends his project of affirming the kinds of creatures we are into the territory of judgment and human error: nobody is beyond judging or beyond making mistakes, yet people build elaborate strategies to avoid both. Clamence, who looks like the picture of the lucid rebel, undergoes a reverse baptism that reveals his morality as performative, and he responds with the judge-penitent strategy of condemning himself before anyone else can. Camus locates the source of such escapes in the modern condition Kafka depicted, where people outsource their morality to faceless officials, and he argues the lucid response is compassion; still, he rejects even Kafka's strange, inaccessible form of hope, wanting to affirm only what we can actually know.
keyIdeas: The Fall carries the argument of the Myth of Sisyphus, The Plague, and The Rebel into judgment and human error, insisting that nobody is beyond judgment or beyond making mistakes.

Clamence's reverse baptism is a series of moments, not one purifying dunk, that reveal how morally questionable and performative his apparent goodness really is, and his judge-penitent confession judges himself first so others have nothing left to condemn.

Kafka is an artist rather than a system-building philosopher, comparable to Zeno of ancient Greece: powerful images that indirectly moved philosophy forward, with a deliberately confusing style that recreates the feeling of confronting the absurd head on.

Joseph K's compliance with his arrest mirrors modern people who outsource morality and decision-making to officials, parties, or causes, which is why Camus wants politics shrunk back to housekeeping instead of supplying entire worldviews.

Since nobody is born into the Mediterranean sun, people who grab escape strategies are desperate rather than evil, so compassion is solidarity at the level of guilt and judgment; even so, Camus rejects Kafka's deferred hope because it traps people in an infinite search for grace.

terms.def: A series of moments in Clamence's life that, instead of morally purifying him, reveal how morally questionable he truly is.
Clamence's strategy of acting as judge and prisoner at once, confessing his own badness first so nobody else can judge him and his later judgments of others swing upward.
Kafka's deliberate style of dense symbolism and constant reader confusion that recreates the experience of facing a world exceeding our rational expectations.
Camus's name for the hope Kafka writes into his books, which always lies outside what human beings could ever actually access and is constantly deferred.

terms.term: Embracing the God that consumes them
terms.def: Camus's phrase for surrendering to a party, philosophy, or god that lets people keep living without facing their existence in lucid revolt.

anchors: That nobody out there is BEYOND judgement or BEYOND making mistakes.

instead of there being a moment, where he’s dunked in water, that morally purifies him…he has a series of moments in his life…that REVEAL to him JUST how much of a morally QUESTIONABLE person he truly is
If I just cut MYSELF down enough and tell you all the bad things about me…then YOU don’t have anything left that you can JUDGE me for.
Zeno…NO doubt helped MOVE philosophy forward indirectly…and well: this is how I think of Kafka’s place in modernity as well.
Because the WAY you feel when you read a Kafka novel to Camus…IS the way you feel sometimes… when you confront the ABSURDITY of the universe, head on.
his SOLUTION…is to just OUTSOURCE his DECISION making about what to do next, to outsource his MORALITY…to the officials that always tell him the next place to be
It’s about doing the sort of BACKGROUND stuff…that then allows for the actual PEOPLE… to go about living their lives, CREATING what the society is that they live in.
That maybe compassion is the equivalent of solidarity…AT the level of guilt and judgment.
It’s hope in a strange form from Kafka…because it ALWAYS lies outside… of what WE as human beings…could ever actually have access to.
Camus wants to affirm EVERYTHING he thinks we can know about the world…and that doesn’t include a mysterious HOPE that we REALLY have no reason to be believing in.
He’s a lawyer. He only takes on cases where he helps the downtrodden of society. In his spare time he likes to help old ladies cross the street, he does balloon animals for the kids.
But of course this whole STRATEGY… is CENTERED on the idea that by just not doing bad THINGS…you somehow DEFAULT into being a GOOD person.
because they never tell me things that would make me have to confront my own limitations as a person.
he WROTE this book The Fall, in PART as an ENDICTMENT on his generation and the strategies they were USING.

Kafka, is someone who’s inspired by Dostoevsky, LOVED his writing, where he’s living almost a full generation AFTER he did his work…but then KAFKA… is doing HIS work, almost a full generation before Camus
There’s one author that compares the impact that Kafka has had on modern thought…to the impact that Shakespeare or Dante had during THEIR times.
This is a scene that just HAPPENS in the middle of the book with no explanation.

Fast forward to him showing up to the attic of an apartment building for his court date, you know the one they didn’t give him a time and place for…and the first thing they say to him when he gets there is good, you’re here, finally! You’re an hour and a half LATE!

Maybe ONE possibility… is that Camus would’ve went in a more… Anarchist direction later in life…. though obviously not GROUNDING any of this “system” in the RIGHTS that people have to self-organization.

Is it to accept the total SILENCE of the universe and the limitations of meaning? Or is it to accept the limitations of my own phenomenological experience…and the possibilities that may lie BEYOND it, that I may catch glimpses of in strange moments?
